taxonomy_dimensions.authority_boundary: Taxonomy dimensions are analytic labels for grouping candidate exception evidence. They do not prove an incident occurred, authorize learning promotion, or override event_type policy. Backfill classifications remain path-signal candidates until source-reviewed or human-confirmed.

detection_mode.description: How the exception is usually detected without collecting raw private evidence.

impact_domain.description: The main risk created if the exception is ignored.

learning_route.description: The safest first route for turning the exception into durable learning.

default_handling.description: The default operational handling before local source authority decides a fix.

review_priority.description: Default urgency for triage queues before severity-specific overrides.

event_types.description: An agent, CI job, hook, or human-run command exited non-zero.
A command timed out, hung, or exceeded a repo-defined runtime budget.
A test failed with enough metadata to identify the suite, not raw private output.
never_collect: raw assertion body containing private rows

event_types.description: A test suite or single test exceeded expected runtime.
A CI workflow failed, flaked, or timed out.
A CLI, app, service, or script raised a runtime exception.
A registry, schema, config, or generated artifact failed validation.
A JSONL row was malformed and had to be quarantined by hash.
A generated report, graph, manifest, or registry derivative is stale.
never_collect: raw artifact when large or private

event_types.description: A report was reused, trusted, or compared without freshness proof.
never_collect: raw report body if it may include private output

event_types.description: A governed artifact exists or changed but was not registered across the manifests, suites, generated snapshots, AI navigation, catalogs, or maps that make it operationally discoverable.
examples: new validator not added to cadence suite
new governed asset missing from AI front door and TOC
schema or harness added without manifest/catalog/map registration

event_types.description: Mail or exception delivery was held in central quarantine.
A duplicate mail delivery was acknowledged rather than redelivered.
examples: same mail id already in inbox

event_types.description: DAD blocked or should have blocked a write to a protected repo.
Enrollment or update was blocked because a repo had uncommitted work.
A packet or recommendation was held before public-facing delivery.
Private, internal, restricted, or unknown-origin data attempted to reach a public-facing repo.
examples: private exception mail routed to public repo

event_types.description: Best-effort screening detected credential-like or PII-like content.
A long raw blob, table-like row, stack trace, transcript, or large output was rejected.
examples: raw log pasted into exception summary

event_types.description: A packet includes instruction-like text that must remain inert evidence.
A red-team, premortem, code-review, security, Claude, Fable, Codex, or human finding.
A plausible future failure story from a premortem review.
A DAD recommendation was harmful, misleading, unsafe, or wasteful.
A repo attempted to use a DAD asset, harness, skill, or template and it failed.
A required or high-priority DAD recommendation was ignored or bypassed.
examples: preflight surfaced rule but task skipped it

event_types.description: An AI agent violated or nearly violated an operating rule.
Rust shadow tests and native Python tests disagreed or coverage was unverified.
Pytest runtime or orchestration evidence shows a slow-test improvement candidate.
Dependency resolution, install, build, or external IO failed.
A required local tool, CLI, plugin, skill, or executable was unavailable in the active environment.
A local environment setting, runtime path, interpreter, or config file was missing or mispointed.
A file, process, network, or repo operation was blocked by permissions or policy.
A network, connector, API, browser, GitHub, email, cloud, or research service failed or was unavailable.
A data import, parse, normalization, extraction, or source-mapping step failed or produced unusable candidate data.
Two or more candidate identities, repo IDs, asset IDs, person records, matter refs, or lineage records conflict.
An agent, script, generated artifact, or DAD recommendation conflicted with a source repo's authority boundary.
examples: generated report treated as source truth
DAD suggestion would overwrite local authority

event_types.description: Generated or AI-authored code failed compile, typecheck, lint, build, or static validation.
A package, artifact, release, wheel, bundle, image, or deployment build failed.
Synthetic, fixture, golden, or mock data failed to cover a required behavior or created false confidence.
A repo's DAD capture surface, enrollment contract, or local agent guidance predates current DAD capture requirements.
A graph, taxonomy, ontology, edge registry, or schema-derived map drifted from reviewed source definitions.
Mail, upgrade notices, or exception-derived recommendations risk spamming repos or exceeding review budgets.
External code, assets, research, zip imports, generated artifacts, or copied material lacked license/provenance review.
Agent instructions, prompts, skills, or managed blocks drifted from current DAD guidance or conflicted across AI environments.
A repo rename or path move affects DAD return addresses, repo IDs, or usage history.
A repo split or copy creates multiple authority surfaces that need new enrollment records.
examples: copied repo retained old integration id
split repo needs new return address

event_types.description: Roadmap state, acceptance evidence, or validation gate disagreed with reality.
A change could not be validated because a required command, dependency, or environment was missing.
A change was rolled back or reverted after causing a failure or governance concern.
A metadata-only historical candidate discovered by path/name keyword scan.
Fallback event type for packets that need taxonomy review.
examples: new exception pattern not yet classified

backfill_classifier.authority_boundary: Backfill classification is path/name-signal-only candidate evidence. It never reads file contents, never proves an exception occurred, and never promotes learning without review or source-repo confirmation.

rules.false_positive_risk: A parity-named document may be planning notes rather than a real mismatch.
applies_when: Path names mention Rust shadow, parity mismatch, or native/shadow comparison.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a generic parity concept with no test, shadow, or migration context.

rules.false_positive_risk: Slow-test docs can be optimization plans rather than observed timeouts.
applies_when: Path names mention pytest timeout, slow test, or test runtime overrun.
does_not_apply_when: The path only documents desired test performance without a failure signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: The word hang may refer to UI layout or prose rather than a stuck command.
applies_when: Path names suggest a command, process, or workflow timed out or hung.
does_not_apply_when: The path term is unrelated prose, design language, or fixture noise.

rules.false_positive_risk: A tool-unavailable path may describe a fallback design, not an observed missing tool.
applies_when: Path names mention a missing CLI, command-not-found, not-on-PATH, or unavailable tool.
does_not_apply_when: The file is a generic install guide without failure or fallback context.

rules.false_positive_risk: Config-named files may be normal setup docs rather than exceptions.
applies_when: Path names point to missing environment, PYTHONPATH, runtime, or local config.
does_not_apply_when: The path is the authoritative config itself and not evidence of a missing config.

rules.false_positive_risk: Protection docs can be intentional policy rather than a failed operation.
applies_when: Path names mention denied access, forbidden operations, or protected writes.
does_not_apply_when: The path only documents a normal permission model without an exception signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: External-service docs can be runbooks or tests rather than observed outages.
applies_when: Path names mention API, connector, network, rate-limit, GitHub, Cloudflare, or service unavailable failures.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal integration guide without a failure marker.

rules.false_positive_risk: Parser and import names may refer to normal code paths or tests.
applies_when: Path names mention import, ingestion, parse, extraction, normalization, or data-map failure.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a parser module without a failure, drift, or review marker.

rules.false_positive_risk: Identity conflict terms may be taxonomy examples rather than live conflicts.
applies_when: Path names mention duplicate identities, ID collision, lineage conflict, or matter-link ambiguity.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a glossary or schema that merely defines identity terms.

rules.false_positive_risk: Authority-boundary docs can be preventive guidance rather than actual conflict.
applies_when: Path names mention source authority conflict, authority leak, source truth conflict, or overwrites.
does_not_apply_when: The path only states normal source-authority rules with no incident signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: Compile-error fixtures can be negative tests rather than failed generated code.
applies_when: Path names mention compile, typecheck, mypy, tsc, Rust build, or generated-code failure.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal compiler test fixture and no failure review marker exists.

rules.false_positive_risk: Build-failure paths can be example fixtures or runbooks.
applies_when: Path names mention package, build, wheel, publish, deploy, bundle, or zip artifact failure.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal build script or release checklist without failure language.

rules.false_positive_risk: Test-gap wording can be planned coverage, not an observed false green.
applies_when: Path names mention fixture, synthetic data, golden case, or test gap.
does_not_apply_when: The path is an ordinary test fixture with no gap or missing signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: Capture-surface files may be generated audit outputs, not source repo defects.
applies_when: Path names mention stale or unknown capture surface, capture version gap, or enrollment capture gap.
does_not_apply_when: The path is merely the current capture contract template.

rules.false_positive_risk: Taxonomy drift terms may be roadmap goals rather than stale generated evidence.
applies_when: Path names mention taxonomy, graph, ontology, edge-registry, or graph-edge drift/gap.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal taxonomy or graph source without drift language.

rules.false_positive_risk: Quarantine paths may be expected storage, not a new exception.
applies_when: Path names mention mail quarantine or rejected packet quarantine.
does_not_apply_when: The path is the central quarantine directory itself without a review signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: Notice-budget docs may be policy design rather than observed spam.
applies_when: Path names mention mail spam, notice budgets, duplicate notices, or inbox backpressure.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal mail policy doc with no risk or incident marker.

rules.false_positive_risk: The word stale may appear in unrelated cache or lifecycle docs.
applies_when: Path names mention stale reports, stale artifacts, or stale generated evidence.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal staleness policy without a candidate failure.

rules.false_positive_risk: Registration-gap paths may be planned hardening rather than an observed drift.
applies_when: Path names mention artifact registration drift, manifest enrollment gaps, suite membership gaps, front-door/TOC gaps, or catalog registration gaps.
does_not_apply_when: The path is the canonical registry or catalog without gap language.

rules.false_positive_risk: License or provenance paths may be preventive policy rather than missing review.
applies_when: Path names mention missing license review, provenance gaps, external code review, or zip provenance.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal license file or source registry without gap language.

rules.false_positive_risk: Instruction-drift docs may be intentional migration plans.
applies_when: Path names mention prompt, instruction, managed-block, or skill drift.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a current instruction source with no drift or mismatch signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: Revert paths may document a procedure rather than an actual rollback.
applies_when: Path names mention rollback, rolled-back changes, or revert evidence.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a generic rollback runbook without an incident marker.

rules.false_positive_risk: Package-manager error names can be fixture examples.
applies_when: Path names mention dependency, install, pip, cargo, or npm errors.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a lockfile or normal package-manager config without failure language.

rules.false_positive_risk: Schema validation names can be positive test fixtures.
applies_when: Path names mention schema validation failures, schema errors, or validation errors.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a validator source file with no failure or error signal.

rules.false_positive_risk: Review-finding paths can be review templates or examples.
applies_when: Path names mention review findings, red-team notes, or audit findings.
does_not_apply_when: The path is only a reusable review template with no finding instance.

rules.false_positive_risk: Premortem files may contain planning scenarios rather than observed failures.
applies_when: Path names mention premortems or failure stories.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a generic premortem template without a concrete subsystem.

rules.false_positive_risk: Workflow-failure paths can be workflow tests or examples.
applies_when: Path names mention CI, workflow, or GitHub Actions failures.
does_not_apply_when: The path is a normal workflow file without failure language.

rules.false_positive_risk: Generic failure words are noisy and should be reviewed before any learning promotion.
applies_when: Path names contain generic incident, exception, failure, error, or bug language and no more specific rule matched first.
does_not_apply_when: A more specific reviewed rule matched the same path.
